EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

Developer harness (Eitri)

Eitri is the EDS agentic developer harness. Its 19 steps take one user story from the handed-off product requirements document (PRD) to a compliance-checked technical requirements document (TRD), a set of verified issues, implementation in a self-correcting loop, and closeout with independent evidence.

Steps are ordered by their dependencies and can be adjusted to fit a team’s tooling. The harness is built on Matt Pocock’s engineering workflow, and teams are encouraged to own, adapt and extend it. This page describes what each phase achieves; the skills catalogue names the skill behind each step.

Set up the harness once

Setup is done once for each machine or repository, before delivery work starts. It puts three things in place:

  • Two skill sets. Matt Pocock’s base engineering skills, installed unchanged, and the EDS add-on skills maintained by the CoreX EDS team.
  • The AppStandards library. A shared set of application best-practice documents, on topics such as logging and reporting, that the harness uses during planning.
  • Optionally, the team’s own standards. A team can reference its own standards repository so the agent factors it into each story’s design. Read how a team registers its standards.

The harness can also record token usage and cost locally each time a skill runs. A further capability, in development and not yet available Planned, will review standards documents against current versions of the technologies they cover and apply only the changes a person approves.

See the 19 steps in four phases

Steps 1–6 set up the repository and turn one user story into a TRD. Steps 7–10 check the TRD against standards and policy, slice it into issues and verify them, with a human gate before and after slicing. Steps 11–12 build one issue in the execution mode the team chooses. Steps 13–19 improve the design, extend the architecture tests, review the change and gather browser and end-to-end evidence.

Plan and schedule a story (Steps 1–6)

Planning sets up the tracker and architecture checks once, puts the PRD’s user stories in a build order, and then turns one story at a time into a user story level TRD.

Planning steps and their results
StepWhat happensLabelResult
1Set up the issue tracker, triage labels and where domain documents liveOne-time setupEvery skill reads the same repository configuration
2Sequence the PRD’s user stories by their dependenciesCoreA dependency graph, a planning report for the project manager (PM), a delivery plan for developers, and stories on the tracker in delivery order
3Connect live library documentation through Context7Optional PlannedDocumentation for the exact library versions in the project, so the agent does not rely on outdated training data
4Plan and generate architecture boundary testsOne-time setupRunnable tests, using ArchUnit for Java or dependency-cruiser for TypeScript, so a violation fails the build instead of drifting silently
5Investigate the story and resolve its open design decisionsCoreDecisions recorded in the repository as shared vocabulary and architecture decision records (ADRs)
6Write the user story TRDCoreA TRD on the tracker, ready for checking

Sequence the stories (Step 2)

Sequencing gives two views of the same plan. A PM or business analyst (BA) first builds the dependency graph and the PM Report, which estimates duration and team size and shows the critical path and delivery risks. An architect or Tech Lead then generates the Developer Delivery Plan for a given team size: the build sequence, effort estimates, acceptance criteria and the standards that apply to each story.

Stories can be split into sequential releases of two to three months, and stories added later are merged into the plan without rebuilding it. As issues close, the plan is reconciled against actual progress.

The AppStandards topics matched to stories are logging, file management, interface and batch processing, user access control, multi-factor authentication (MFA), MCC Platform Services (MCNS, MPDS) and reporting. Because each story carries its standards from Step 2, the agent applies them during investigation, before conflicts surface at the standards check.

Investigate, then write the TRD (Steps 5–6)

The developer takes the next story from the delivery plan and resolves its open decisions before anything is written. A large, ambiguous story is broken into investigation tickets and resolved one at a time; a smaller, well-defined story is stress-tested against the domain model in one session.

The TRD then brings the decisions together without further questions. It covers the problem statement, the solution, user stories, implementation decisions, testing decisions and what is out of scope.

Check the TRD and slice it (Steps 7–10)

Before any code is written, the TRD is checked against standards and policy and signed off. It is then sliced into tracer-bullet issues: thin vertical slices, each reaching an observable outcome through every layer it needs. The issues are verified and approved before implementation starts.

Checking and slicing steps and their results
StepWhat happensLabelResult
7Compare the TRD with the AppStandards attached to the storyCoreGaps rated Critical or Warning, a recorded decision for each, and a pass or fail report
8Audit the TRD against IM8 and ARC controlsCoreOne verdict for each control and a compliance report
Human gate 1A person signs off the TRDHITL 1The design is compliance-approved and cleared for slicing
9Slice the TRD into issuesCoreIssues on the tracker with explicit dependencies, each small enough for one agent session and demonstrable on its own
10Verify the issuesCoreEach issue questioned against eight quality criteria, and the set checked for coverage, overlap and sound dependencies
Human gate 2A person approves the issuesHITL 2The issues are execution-ready and development can begin

The compliance audit covers two policy sets. Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) is the Singapore Government’s ICT security policy; the audit uses its application technical controls. The Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC) is GovTech’s governance framework for risks in agentic AI systems.

Each control is judged as met, fixable by tightening the wording, failed, deferred to implementation because it cannot be checked at specification stage, or not applicable. Planning is not complete while any control is failed.

Because every issue declares what blocks it, several agents or developers can work on different issues in parallel safely.

Choose an execution mode

All three modes run the same build loop on one execution-ready issue. They differ in who operates it and how much happens without a person watching.

Execution modes for the build loop
ModeWho runs itHow it works
1. Local interactiveThe developer, locallyThe developer works with the agent as a pair programmer, reviewing and directing its decisions in real time.
2. Local autonomousThe developer, through a local autonomous agentAn isolated sandbox workspace checks out the code, runs the build loop end to end and commits locally, with no interaction during the run.
3. Cloud or CI autonomousA GitLab pipeline or cloud runnerThe pipeline detects an execution-ready issue, runs the build loop, pushes the changes, opens a merge request (MR) and triggers an automated review that posts comments for the developer.

Choose a mode for each issue based on how well specified it is and how much control and evidence surround it; read how to increase autonomy with evidence.

Build one issue in a self-correcting loop (Steps 11–12)

Scaffold the interface first, if there is a prototype (Step 11) Optional

For a feature delivered with a design or HTML prototype, the harness can generate interface components before the loop begins. Conversion from a Google Stitch project is available; conversion from a standalone HTML file is not yet available Planned. The output is structural scaffolding, not production-ready code. The developer connects state, data and API contracts during the build loop.

Implement one issue (Step 12) Core

The build loop is run by the /do-work skill. It adapts Matt Pocock’s implementation skill, which reviews once at the end. Instead, the loop keeps reviewing and correcting until no must-fix findings remain, and then runs validation gates for the technology stack.

Before writing code, the agent reads the issue, the relevant architecture decisions and the codebase, and confirms that acceptance criteria are in place. The inner loop then implements, writing tests first where the code carries logic, and reviews the result against the issue and its acceptance criteria. If must-fix findings remain, it fixes them and implements again.

When the exit check is clear, Gates 1 and 2 run in parallel; any failure returns to Fix. After they pass, the optional mutation gate runs. The agent then commits only that issue’s changes, posts a comment summarising what it implemented and verified, and closes the issue.

Validation gates in the build loop, with the harness’s default thresholds; teams can change them
GateWhat it checksBlocks when
1. Compile and test CoreFormatting, type checks or compilation, tests with coverage, and a production build, for TypeScript and Java.Any check fails, or test coverage is below 80%
2. Quality and compliance CoreIndependent reviews run in parallel: a review against coding standards and the specification, Semgrep static security analysis, IM8 security controls, the thermo-nuclear maintainability review maintained by Cursor, and React and Spring framework reviews. A Sonar review is not yet available Planned.Any Critical or High finding
3. Mutation testing Optional · RecommendedIntroduces deliberate faults into changed files, using PIT for Java or StrykerJS for TypeScript, to check that the tests detect them.Mutation score below 70%

Architecture boundary tests are not a gate inside the loop; the feature’s tests are generated at Step 14.

Toward an AI software factory

The harness describes an AI software factory as a self-steering delivery engine: agents pick up issues, implement and validate them against a defined quality bar, commit and close them. Running the build loop in Mode 2 or Mode 3 is the harness’s route to this. Because Step 9 publishes issues with explicit dependencies, several agents can take different issues in parallel. Read the software factory concept.

Teams own the factory’s quality bar by treating the build loop as configuration they maintain. They can add a gate, such as a new scanner or performance check; tighten a threshold, such as coverage or mutation score; or add reviewers for their own domain. Raising the bar this way does not change the delivery workflow.

Verify and close out (Steps 13–19)

After the loop commits the implementation, closeout improves the design, extends architecture tests, reviews the change against standards and the specification, and collects browser and end-to-end evidence before the merge request is approved.

Closeout steps
StepWhat happensLabel
13Find shallow modules in recently changed areas and propose how to deepen themOptional · Recommended
14Extend the architecture boundary tests to cover the new featureCore
15Review the change against coding standards and against the specification, in two independent reviewsCore
16Diagnose hard bugs or performance regressions through a structured six-phase methodOptional
17Check acceptance criteria in a live browser through agent-browser, with screenshotsOptional · Recommended
18Commit the closeout artefacts as logically grouped commitsOptional · Recommended
19Turn the user story into repeatable Playwright end-to-end tests with fresh evidenceOptional · Recommended

The Step 15 review runs its two parts separately, so neither influences the other. One compares the change with the repository’s documented coding standards, falling back to a baseline of common code smells. The other compares it with the originating issue or TRD, flagging missing requirements, scope creep and requirements that look implemented but are wrong.

End-to-end evidence builds up one user story at a time. A run counts only after its final verifier passes, and a stability check can repeat it at least three times to flag results that change between runs. A failing run does not block a push unless the repository adds a pipeline gate.

Each check writes its report to the repository, so reviewers can inspect the evidence behind a decision: the dependency graph, the architecture test plan, the compliance and review reports, browser screenshots and end-to-end results.

Definition of done for planning and implementation

A story is ready to move on when the following hold. The thresholds are the harness defaults; teams can change them.

Planning is done (Steps 1–10) when

  • The standards check reports no Critical gaps against AppStandards.
  • The compliance audit reports no failed controls, wording fixes have been applied, and deferred controls are tracked into implementation.
  • HITL 1 The TRD has been reviewed, its gaps resolved and signed off before slicing.
  • Every issue is confirmed as a true tracer bullet: vertical, demonstrable and well specified.
  • HITL 2 The issues have been reviewed, open questions resolved and approved for execution.

Implementation is done (Steps 12–19) when

  • Formatting, type checks, tests and the build pass, with at least 80% test coverage.
  • Project and feature architecture boundary tests pass.
  • The quality and compliance gate reports no Critical or High findings.
  • Optionally, the mutation score on changed files is at least 70%.
  • The implementation is committed and the issue is closed with a verification comment.
  • The Step 15 review passes on both coding standards and the specification.
  • Optionally, acceptance criteria are verified in a live browser and story end-to-end evidence is produced.

Next step: to see what happens once a merge request is ready, follow the path to production. For the skill behind each step, open the skills catalogue.
